Name: The Roman Dictatorship: Six Months of Absolute Power and the Check of the Master of the Horse
RagShortTexts: When both consuls fell or suffered defeat, the Senate had a dictator appointed to exercise supreme, absolute rule
The axes of his twenty-four lictors were not removed even inside the city, displaying unlimited power over life and death, but his term was limited to half a year
The check of his deputy, the Master of the Horse, and his lack of control over the treasury prevented a return of tyranny
BaseText: For the desperate situation in which a consul had fallen or command on the battlefield had collapsed into chaos and paralysis, the Roman constitution established the office of 'dictator' (Dictator). The dictator was appointed by a consul on the instruction of the Senate, and his term was usually strictly limited to no more than six months. The dictator held supreme and comprehensive military and civil authority (Imperium Maius); the twenty-four lictors escorting him did not need to remove the axes from their bundles of rods even inside the sacred boundary of the city of Rome (Pomerium), and his rulings could not be appealed to a court. To prevent the dictator from becoming a tyrant for life, the constitution set up close checks: the dictator had to appoint a plebeian or a noble of a rival faction as his deputy, the 'Master of the Horse' (Magister Equitum); the dictator had no right to spend a single coin of the treasury, and all military funds had to be granted by the Senate; and once the specific emergency task was completed, he had to resign of his own accord and return home before the six months expired.

Variants.Content: Fabius and Buteo proved the nobility of the dictatorship. To wield a sovereign's power without the selfishness of a usurper, and to go back to the plow once the crisis is settled, this is true Roman virtue!

When Minucius, the Master of the Horse, was given command equal to the dictator's, the plebeians proved to the nobles that even in wartime we will not let a single man monopolize our lives and deaths!
The Romans tamed the terrifying power of tyranny into a constitutional tool valid for six months, a subtle balance that Aristotle never saw in the constitutions of the Greek city-states.
